summary:
Dancing with the SARs is a multi-temporal basin monitoring and early warning web platform built for the metropolitan area of Cochabamba, Bolivia, from the steep
    Tunari mountain range in the north to the Rocha river valley in the south. Our team developed an integrated pipeline that pairs NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band
    polarimetric radar with Sentinel-1 OPERA backscatter, GPM IMERG rainfall, Copernicus 30-meter elevation models, NASA FIRMS thermal anomalies, and municipal
    drainage and emergency layers from Cochabamba. Users can track upcoming satellite passes on a 3D globe, inspect terrain susceptibility and surface water maps,
    monitor deterministic district-level flood and mudflow alerts, and ask natural-language questions by text or voice to receive radar change maps and
    plain-language explanations. Because clouds hide storm damage during the Andean rainy season, all-weather L-band SAR helps civil defense teams and citizens spot
    soil saturation, slope disturbance, and flooding early.
details:
What it does and how it works

Dancing with the SARs combines satellite orbital tracking, hydrological terrain modeling, deterministic early warning alerts, and an on-demand SAR analysis

pipeline in a single web application tailored to Cochabamba, Bolivia.

The Orbit view propagates live Two-Line Orbital Elements from CelesTrak using the SGP4 model on a 3D CesiumJS globe to show real-time positions and 48-hour pass

predictions for NISAR and Sentinel-1 over Cochabamba.

The Basin view clips Copernicus DEM GLO-30 elevation tiles to the Cochabamba watershed, derives slope and topographic concavity, and overlays NASA GPM IMERG and

NASA POWER rainfall, OPERA Dynamic Surface Water Extent from Sentinel-1, NISAR GCOV L-band radar layers, and municipal WMS layers from the Autonomous Municipal

Government of Cochabamba including basins, drainage networks, the 2750-meter urban boundary, district borders, and emergency records. Users can click any

coordinate for point diagnostics and download a preventive markdown bulletin.

The Events view integrates NASA FIRMS active fire detections with NASA GIBS optical, flood, and vegetation layers.

The Alerts view connects over WebSockets to a deterministic alert engine that evaluates 24-hour and 72-hour GPM IMERG rainfall, antecedent precipitation,

terrain ruggedness, and radar evidence against configurable YAML thresholds and historical Bolivian flood and mudflow cases, emitting schema-validated risk

levels with explicit confidence scores that state when satellite passes were unavailable.

The Radar Echoes interface lets users ask questions by text or voice. A Python harness parses the request, queries NASA Earthdata CMR and ASF for NISAR L2 GCOV

HDF5 granules, and switches automatically to Sentinel-1 OPERA RTC-S1 when NISAR coverage over the area is below 70 percent. It streams only the required spatial

subsets over S3 or HTTPS range requests, applies speckle filtering, computes polarimetric indices such as RVI and CPR, extracts drainage sediment corridors from

OpenStreetMap and municipal torrents, detects change hotspots, and outputs 3D globe grids, polygon objects, and plain-language explanations.

Benefits and intended impact

Cochabamba faces recurring mudflows on the Tunari foothills and flash flooding in the Rocha valley during the rainy season, when cloud cover blocks optical

satellites. By translating complex L-band and C-band radar backscatter into clear risk levels, localized maps, and accessible explanations in Spanish and

English, the platform bridges satellite science with municipal technicians, civil defense teams, and local residents.

Tools, languages, and software used

The frontend is built with Angular 22, TypeScript, CesiumJS, MapLibre GL JS, Satellite.js, Transloco, and Ajv. The backend runs on Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn,

Pydantic, Rasterio, Shapely, NumPy, Pillow, earthaccess, asf_search, xarray, h5netcdf, and uv, using JSON Schema contracts and a modular 12-Factor architecture.

External AI services are used strictly for secondary assistance: Anthropic Claude parses natural-language queries and drafts didactic explanations from

deterministic radar metrics, Google Gemini provides a server-side speech-to-text fallback and generated the animated mascot sprites, and browser Web Speech API

supports direct voice input.

Creativity and factors considered

Our team prioritized scientific honesty and bandwidth efficiency. Instead of downloading multi-gigabyte HDF5 scenes, the backend streams spatial chunks over

HTTPS and clips GIBS tiles to the watershed polygon. Every risk score is computed deterministically so language models never invent measurements, and every

alert explicitly reports data gaps and sensor frequency differences between L-band NISAR and C-band Sentinel-1.
